name: Jalpesh Mela at Shivaratri
when: Feb–Mar, around Maha Shivaratri (lunar calendar); pilgrims also come through Shravan (Jul–Aug)
summary: The Shiva temple at Jalpesh near Maynaguri holds one of north Bengal's oldest fairs around Maha Shivaratri. Pilgrims, traders and families from across the Dooars and Cooch Behar fill the fields around the temple for days. It is about 25–30 km from Lataguri.
body: Jalpesh is a Shiva temple a few kilometres from Maynaguri in Jalpaiguri district. Local histories link its building to the Koch kings of Cooch Behar in the 17th century, with later rebuilding by the Raikat rulers of Baikunthapur; the details vary by source, so treat dates you hear on the spot with care. The linga sits below floor level in a pit, which pilgrims reach by stepping down.

The mela grows up around Maha Shivaratri, in February or March, with stalls of bamboo ware, sweets, utensils, toys and clothes, rides for children, and a great deal of jalebi. A second wave of devotees comes in the month of Shravan, many carrying water from the Teesta on foot. It is a working pilgrim fair, not a show, and the crowds are local.

For a Dooars visitor it is an easy half-day from Lataguri. Go early, leave shoes at a stall that keeps them for a few rupees, carry small change, and keep your phone in a front pocket in the crush near the temple gate.
tips: Reach before 8 am on the main Shivaratri day; by noon the approach roads jam.
Dress modestly and expect to remove shoes well before the shrine.
Combine it with an afternoon Gorumara watchtower slot booked in advance from Lataguri.

faqs.a: It centres on Maha Shivaratri, which falls in February or March by the lunar calendar, and the fair runs for several days around it. Exact dates and length are set locally each year, so check current status before you travel. Shravan, in July and August, brings a separate stream of pilgrims but not the full fair.

faqs.q: How do I get to Jalpesh from Lataguri?
faqs.a: Jalpesh is roughly 25–30 km from Lataguri via Maynaguri, about 45 minutes to an hour by car. A hired car for the half-day costs roughly ₹1,500–2,000. On the main festival day, local buses and shared autos from Maynaguri are packed, so a car with a driver who knows the parking fields saves time.

Visitors of other faiths generally walk the fair and the temple grounds without trouble; entry to the inner shrine is a matter for the temple on the day. Dress modestly, remove shoes, follow the queue and ask before photographing people at prayer. Inside the sanctum, photography is usually not allowed.

faqs.q: Is the Jalpesh Mela suitable for children?
faqs.a: Yes, with care. Children enjoy the rides, toy stalls and sweets, but the crowd near the temple gate is dense on Shivaratri. Agree a meeting point, write your phone number on a card in your child's pocket, and keep small children on the fair side rather than in the temple queue.

name: Mahakal Cave at Shivaratri
summary: Each Maha Shivaratri thousands of pilgrims walk up the Jayanti riverbed to the Mahakal cave in the Buxa hills, where limestone formations are worshipped as Shiva. A small fair grows at Jayanti, and the forest path fills with people for one or two days.
body: Mahakal is a limestone cave in the hills above Jayanti, inside the Buxa Tiger Reserve and close to the Bhutan border. Water dripping through the rock has built stalactites and stalagmites, and pilgrims revere these as forms of Shiva. On ordinary days you meet a handful of walkers; at Shivaratri the path becomes a slow procession.

The walk follows the stony bed of the Jayanti river and then climbs to the cave. Most people describe it as about 5–6 km each way, with river crossings that are easy in the dry months; check locally, because the riverbed shifts after every monsoon. Stalls selling tea, puffed rice, flowers and incense appear at Jayanti village and along the lower path.

Forest rules still apply during the festival: stay on the pilgrim route, leave nothing behind, and be out of the forest before dark. The forest department and local committees set the arrangements each year, so check current status before you travel.
tips: Start at first light to walk in cool air and finish before the midday rush.
Wear shoes that can get wet; you cross the river channels several times.
Carry water and a little food, but bring your plastic back down.

faqs.q: How long is the walk to Mahakal cave?
faqs.a: It is usually given as about 5–6 km each way from Jayanti, mostly along the riverbed with a steeper final climb, which takes three to four hours on foot. The riverbed changes after each monsoon, so ask in Jayanti on the day and go with a local guide outside the festival.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to walk to Mahakal?
faqs.a: Mahakal lies inside the Buxa Tiger Reserve, where entry rules apply and change. During Shivaratri the route is open to pilgrims under local arrangements; at other times you may need forest department permission and a guide. Ask at the Rajabhatkhawa or Jayanti forest offices and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where do pilgrims stay during the festival?
faqs.a: Jayanti has a small number of homestays and lodges that fill quickly at Shivaratri. Many visitors come as day-trippers from Alipurduar, about 30 km away, or stay in Rajabhatkhawa or Santalabari. Book a homestay early, or plan a long day from Alipurduar with a car.

faqs.q: Is the Mahakal walk suitable for older people?
faqs.a: It is a long day on uneven, stony ground with river crossings and a steep last section. Fit older walkers manage it slowly; anyone with knee trouble or heart conditions should not attempt it on the crowded festival day. The riverbank at Jayanti itself is an easy and pleasant alternative.

name: Karam Puja in the tea gardens
when: Aug–Sep, in the month of Bhadra (lunar calendar)
summary: Karam is the harvest and kinship festival of the Oraon, Munda and other Adivasi families whose ancestors came to the Dooars tea gardens from Chota Nagpur. Branches of the karam tree are planted, songs are sung through the night and the garden lines dance.
body: When the Dooars tea gardens opened from the 1870s, planters recruited workers from Chota Nagpur and the central Indian hills, and their descendants still form a large part of the garden communities between Malbazar, Birpara and Alipurduar. They brought Karam with them. The festival honours the karam tree, a symbol of fortune and family, and is kept on the eleventh day of the bright half of Bhadra.

Young women fast, branches of the tree are set up in the courtyard or the open ground of the garden lines, and an elder tells the story of Karma and Dharma. Then the drums (mandar and dhol) start and the dancing goes on late into the night. In many gardens around Madarihat and Birpara the whole labour line joins in.

This is a community festival, not a tourist event. If a host family or garden staff invites you, go, sit where you are told, ask before photographing, and accept whatever is offered. Parks are closed in this season, so a Karam visit pairs with a rainy-season stay in a tea garden homestay.
tips: Go only with an invitation from a family or someone who lives in the garden lines.
Ask before taking any photograph, and never use flash during the rituals.
Monsoon roads are slippery; travel in daylight and keep spare days.

faqs.q: When is Karam Puja celebrated in the Dooars?
faqs.a: Karam falls on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Bhadra, which lands in August or September. Celebrations in the tea gardens often spread across the evening and night, sometimes longer. Dates shift each year with the lunar calendar, so ask a local contact for the exact day before you plan.

faqs.q: Can tourists attend Karam in a tea garden?
faqs.a: Only as guests. Karam is held in family courtyards and the garden lines, not on a stage. Travellers who stay in a garden homestay or have a local friend are often welcomed. Turn up with an invitation, follow your host's lead, and do not wander into garden lines alone at night.

faqs.q: Why is Karam celebrated in the Dooars tea gardens?
faqs.a: Many garden workers' families descend from people recruited from Chota Nagpur, in present-day Jharkhand and nearby areas, after the gardens opened from 1874. They kept their language, songs and festivals, and Karam remains one of the most important. It is a festival of the soil, siblings and good fortune.

faqs.q: Is August a good time to visit the Dooars?
faqs.a: For wildlife, no: Jaldapara, Gorumara and the other parks close from about mid-June to mid-September. For green tea gardens, low prices, Karam and Jhulan festivities, it can be rewarding if you accept rain, leeches and road delays. Check current status before you travel.
